# Industrial Services Unit — Turnaround-or-Exit Assessment and Twelve-Month Plan

*Part II: Segmentation, Plan, Exit Architecture and Decision Rules*

---

## 1. The Decision Architecture (read this first)

| | |
|---|---|
| **What is being decided** | Not "turnaround or exit." It is: *what is the defensible core, and who should own it?* |
| **When it is decided** | **Month 6–7**, not Month 12. A sale process needs 6–9 months; a wind-down needs 9–15. Deciding in Month 11 is choosing a distressed outcome. |
| **What runs until then** | A single dual-track program. ~80% of turnaround work = sale-readiness work. Divergent decisions are named now and *deliberately deferred* to the gate. |
| **What is done in Week 1** | Management retention. Everything else is unexecutable without it. |
| **What must never happen** | A third across-the-board cost program. Two have proven the losses are not in overhead. |

**Four possible endings, all acceptable, one unacceptable:**

- **A. Fix and keep** — core earns >12% ROCE and strategically anchors the group's customer relationships.
- **B. Fix and sell** — core earns 5–7% but doesn't deserve group capital or management bandwidth. *This is the most likely best outcome.*
- **C. Fix the core, sell it, wind down the rest** — partial carve-out plus orderly run-off of the loss engine.
- **D. Orderly exit now** — if the Month 3 fact base shows no profitable core at all.
- **Unacceptable: Month 12 arrives with an unproven core, no management team, and a fire-sale.**

---

## 2. Diagnosis: The Verdict Logic and the 100-Day Fact Base

### 2.1 The expected finding

The prior analysis establishes the tests. The expected verdict — in perhaps 80% of units with this signature — is **mixed, in a specific and highly actionable pattern**:

> **Structurally unattractive** in lump-sum capital project work and labour supply (roughly a third of revenue, no willingness to pay, uncapped downside, no right to win). **Execution-broken but structurally sound** in recurring maintenance, inspection and compliance-driven specialty services (pricing not escalated, change orders not collected, branch density diluted, supervision hollowed out by the two prior cost programs).

This verdict does not license a "turnaround." It licenses **portfolio surgery followed by re-underwriting the remainder as a new business.** The distinction matters: a turnaround defends the revenue base; surgery deliberately destroys 25–35% of it.

### 2.2 The 100-day fact base — five workstreams, hard deliverables

| # | Workstream | Deliverable by Day 100 | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Contract-level truth** | Fully-loaded contribution margin for 100% of revenue by contract: true equipment charge, mobilisation, rework/warranty, working-capital carry, supervision. Bid-vintage view (are losses in legacy 2021–22 bids or in current pricing?). | CFO + external forensic support |
| 2 | **Loss-to-cash reconciliation** | 3 years of reported EBITDA vs. operating cash flow, bridged line by line. Quantify unbilled change orders, POC revenue, contract assets, retentions, deferred maintenance. | CFO |
| 3 | **Group interdependency audit** | The quantified answer to the shared-customer veto (§4.2). Signed off by *each* profitable division head. | Group strategy, not the unit |
| 4 | **Market and win/loss** | Peer margin benchmark (6–10 independents), win rate by price percentile, reasons-lost file, density/share by geography. | Commercial director + external |
| 5 | **Exit-cost floor** | The net cash cost of orderly closure — the reservation price below which no sale is worth doing. | CFO + legal |

**Workstream 5 is the most commonly skipped and most valuable.** Until you know that closure costs, say, $85M net (redundancy, lease exits, warranty tails, bonding release, stranded group costs, dis-synergies), you cannot rationally evaluate a bid of "zero plus liability assumption" — which for a loss-making services unit is often a genuinely good outcome worth $85M.

**Rule:** no remediation spend beyond retention and safety until Workstreams 1 and 2 are complete.

---

## 3. Illustrative Economics (the shape of the answer)

| Service line | Revenue | CM % | CM $ | Attached fixed cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Recurring maintenance & inspection | $120M | 26% | $31M | Low | **Core — defend** |
| Specialty / compliance technical services | $50M | 32% | $16M | Low | **Core — grow** |
| Turnaround & shutdown projects | $110M | 12% | $13M | Medium | **Shrink to anchor sites** |
| Lump-sum capital installation | $90M | –4% | –$4M | **High** | **Exit** |
| Labour supply / staffing | $30M | 5% | $1.5M | Low | **Exit or reprice hard** |
| **Total** | **$400M** | **14.4%** | **$58M** | **$75M** | **EBIT ≈ –$17M** |

**Value bridge, –$17M → +$20M:**

| Step | Action | EBIT impact | Timing |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Baseline | –$17M | — |
| 1 | Exit lump-sum installation + labour supply ($120M revenue out) | +$2.5M CM lost, but **+$20–22M** avoidable attached fixed cost removed | Months 2–9 |
| 2 | Repricing: escalation clauses restored, 2–3 pts on recurring; exit or reprice bottom-decile contracts | **+$6–8M** | Months 3–12 |
| 3 | Change-order and claims discipline (project controls, not headcount) | **+$3–4M** | Months 2–8 |
| 4 | Branch rationalisation to dense geographies; overhead resized *to surviving revenue* | **+$5–6M** | Months 6–12 |
| 5 | Specialty growth at 32% CM | **+$2–3M** | Months 9–18 |
| | **Pro-forma: ~$280M revenue, EBIT $18–20M (6–7%)** | | Month 18–24 run-rate |

**And the bigger prize:** a **one-time release of $40–60M** of working capital and disposal proceeds (unbilled receivables, retentions, contract assets, heavy plant, freed leases). For a group, this transforms ROCE and the exit calculus far more than the P&L line does — and it is available under *both* tracks.

---

## 4. Segmentation: Where Profit Can Be Sustained

### 4.1 Service-line screen — three gates, all must pass

1. **Right to win** — density, installed base, regulatory qualification, or technical credential a competitor cannot cheaply replicate.
2. **Willingness to pay** — the customer's cost of failure exceeds our price by an order of magnitude (compliance, safety, unplanned-downtime avoidance = yes; body-shopping and lump-sum installation = no).
3. **Risk symmetry** — downside capped, escalation protected, change orders contractually recoverable.

Recurring, compliance-driven service on an installed base you already touch passes all three. **Fixed-price capital project work almost never passes gate 3 — it is the standard loss engine in industrial services, and it consumes the estimating, PM, heavy-plant and bonding capacity that the profitable lines are charged for.**

### 4.2 Customer screen — and dismantling the shared-customer veto

| | **Low group linkage** | **High group linkage** |
|---|---|---|
| **Profitable to serve** | **Core.** Defend, deepen, use as references. | **Crown jewels.** Protect absolutely; these justify the unit's existence and set the floor on any exit structure. |
| **Unprofitable to serve** | **Exit now.** No debate, no veto available. Fastest, cleanest value creation in the entire plan. | **The real battleground.** Reprice first. If the customer refuses, the *group* must decide — and pay — explicitly. |

**The bottom-right quadrant is where the money is being lost, and it must be resolved with arithmetic, not assertion.** Four steps:

1. **Measure the overlap properly.** For each shared customer: unit revenue and CM; group revenue and *gross profit* from other divisions; whether a single procurement authority makes a bundled decision; whether any MSA, cross-default or bundled-pricing clause legally links the relationships. In practice, genuine bundled buying is typically **10–25% of the claimed overlap** — different buyers, different budgets, different sites.
2. **Audit the hidden subsidy.** Compare shared-account pricing to standalone-account pricing for equivalent scope. The gap is a group-level transfer the group never approved, sitting in the unit's P&L. Quantify it and disclose it to the board as what it is: *an unbudgeted intra-group subsidy.*
3. **Make the group pay for what it wants.** Any contract retained below cost for group-relationship reasons is either (a) repriced, (b) formally cross-charged to the benefiting division, or (c) exited. There is no fourth option. This single rule usually resolves 70% of the veto within 60 days, because divisions defend overlap enthusiastically until they must fund it.
4. **Sign the residual.** Each division head signs a one-page statement of the group gross profit *genuinely* contingent on the unit's continued ownership. That number — likely far smaller than feared — becomes an explicit input to the exit valuation, not a rhetorical trump card.

Where the linkage is real, note that **exit does not sever it.** A long-term preferred-vendor or subcontract agreement with the buyer, or an internal transfer of the core into the division that owns the customer, preserves the relationship without preserving the losses.

---

## 5. The Binding Constraint: Management Retention (Week 1)

The unit is being asset-stripped by the group's own internal labour market. No plan survives that.

| Action | Detail | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| **Transfer freeze** | Group HR blocks internal transfers out of the top 40 roles without CEO-level approval. Unilateral, immediate. | Week 1 |
| **Retention pool** | 1.5–2.5% of revenue ($6–10M), cash, paid at Month 7 (gate) and Month 13. **Outcome-neutral: pays in full on turnaround *or* on completed sale/orderly exit.** This is the critical design feature — otherwise managers rationally sabotage one track. | Week 1–2 |
| **Sale-participation overlay** | For the top 10: a defined share of exit proceeds *and* a defined bonus on hitting the turnaround EBIT gate. Removes the incentive to hide bad news or to fear success. | Week 2–3 |
| **Honesty with the top 10** | Tell them the dual track exists. They will infer it anyway; concealment converts your leadership team into your biggest leak risk and destroys credibility on the one thing you need — truthful contract data. | Week 2 |
| **Backfill the delivery machine** | The prior cuts removed supervision, planning and estimating. Selectively *re-add* 15–25 frontline supervisory and project-controls roles in the core lines. This is the one place headcount goes up. | Months 2–5 |
| **Career guarantee** | Written commitment: on exit, group-wide redeployment rights for the top 40; on turnaround, defined progression. | Month 1 |

---

## 6. Twelve-Month Milestone Map

### Phase 0 — Stabilise (Weeks 1–4)
- Retention package executed; transfer freeze live.
- **Bid moratorium** on all lump-sum capital work and any contract below hurdle CM. Immediate, unconditional. Stops adding to the fire.
- Cash control: daily cash, 13-week rolling forecast, capex freeze except safety and revenue-critical.
- Safety review — downsizing periods are when incidents spike, and one fatality ends both tracks.
- Board reset: agree the Month 6–7 gate, the gate criteria (§8), and that "fix and sell" is a success.
- Appoint dual-track leads: turnaround lead (COO), separation/exit lead (CFO or dedicated), one accountable executive over both.

### Phase 1 — Fact base and first cuts (Months 2–3)
- Five diagnostic workstreams complete (§2.2). **Day 100: verdict paper to board — structural / execution / mixed, with the defensible core defined at contract level.**
- Exit initiated on unprofitable / low-linkage customers (no veto available) — typically 8–12% of revenue.
- Change-order and claims recovery task force live on the existing project backlog; this is early, high-certainty cash.
- Repricing campaign launched on recurring contracts: escalation restoration, bottom-decile renegotiation.
- Vendor data room opened *internally* as "standalone readiness" — carve-out P&L, TSA scoping, legal entity map, contract assignability review. Presented internally as good management hygiene, which it is.

### Phase 2 — Surgery and proof (Months 4–6)
- Lump-sum installation line: no new bids, orderly completion of existing work, plant disposal program, bonding and parent-guarantee run-off plan agreed with sureties.
- Labour supply: repriced or exited.
- Branch rationalisation decisions taken for the surviving footprint; overhead resized *to surviving revenue* — the opposite of the prior across-the-board programs.
- Shared-customer resolution complete; divisional sign-offs obtained.
- **Confidential market sounding**: 3–5 strategic acquirers and 2–3 sponsors approached via adviser, no-names basis, to establish indicative value ranges and structures.
- Exit-cost floor finalised.

### **Month 6–7 — THE GATE** (see §8)
Board decides: Track A (keep and fix), Track B (fix-and-sell / carve-out), or Track D (orderly exit). All prior work supports all three.

### Phase 3a — If turnaround (Months 7–12)
- Deliver positive run-rate EBIT by Month 10–11; book-to-bill >1.0 in core lines.
- Reinvest: specialty capability, sales hiring, systems for job costing and pricing discipline (the absence of which caused this).
- Re-underwrite as a new business: 3-year plan with capital request judged on its own merits against group hurdle rate — *not* on sunk history.

### Phase 3b — If exit (Months 7–15)
- Months 7–8: adviser mandated, information memorandum, management presentations rehearsed.
- Months 9–11: process run; indicative bids; shortlist; confirmatory diligence.
- Months 12–14: SPA negotiation, TSA, regulatory/works-council consultation, preferred-vendor agreements protecting crown-jewel relationships.
- Month 14–15: close. Retained-liability management thereafter (warranty tails, bonds, environmental).

---

## 7. Exit Alternatives

| Option | Structure | Realistic value | Best when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Whole-unit trade sale** | Sale to a services consolidator | Only credible **after** surgery. Pre-surgery: nominal or negative EV (buyer prices the loss-making lines and liabilities). Post-surgery: 5–7× EBITDA on the core. | Core proven, buyer wants scale/density |
| **2. Carve-out sale of the core** | Sell recurring + specialty ($170M rev, ~$15–18M EBITDA); wind down projects internally | Highest gross proceeds (**~$80–120M**) but group retains the closure cost of the rest | Buyers want the annuity, not the project risk |
| **3. Book-of-business / contract sale** | Sell contracts, customer lists, technicians and local assets by geography to 2–4 regional buyers | $30–60M in aggregate; avoids entity-level liability transfer | No single buyer for the whole; strong regional clusters |
| **4. MBO / sponsor deal** | Retained management, vendor loan, earn-out, group as anchor customer | Modest upfront, meaningful deferred; **highest execution certainty** because the buyer already knows the assets | Management is strong and committed; external buyers are scarce |
| **5. Internal transfer** | Fold the core into the profitable division whose customers it serves; close the rest | No cash proceeds, but eliminates the shared-customer objection entirely and captures real commercial synergy | Group linkage proves genuinely material |
| **6. JV / partial sale** | 50/50 with a larger operator who contributes density and takes management control | Deconsolidation, retained upside, relationship preserved | Sub-scale but strategically relevant |
| **7. Orderly solvent wind-down** | Complete backlog, novate contracts, sell assets, redeploy people, preferred-vendor agreements for crown jewels | **Net cost**, e.g. $60–90M, partly offset by $40–60M working-capital release and disposals | No profitable core exists at any scale |
| **8. Sale-leaseback / asset monetisation** | Applies under *any* track | $20–40M cash | Always evaluate; funds the turnaround without group capital |

**Two rules on exit:**
- **Sequence matters more than option choice.** Every option is worth dramatically more after the loss-making lines are gone. Selling in Month 3 destroys value; the surgery *is* the deal preparation.
- **The wind-down cost is the reservation price.** If orderly closure costs $75M net, a bid of "$0 with full liability assumption" is worth $75M. Boards routinely reject such bids on optics and then spend the $75M anyway.

---

## 8. The Month 6–7 Gate: Explicit Criteria

**All five hard gates must pass for Track A or B (fix). Any two failing → Track D (exit now).**

| # | Gate | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Proven profitable core** | ≥$150M revenue at ≥18% contribution margin, demonstrated on *actual* contract-level data for ≥2 consecutive quarters — not forecast |
| 2 | **Demand** | Core-lines book-to-bill ≥1.0 and improving; ≥85% renewal rate on recurring contracts; no loss of a crown-jewel account |
| 3 | **Run-rate profitability visible** | Positive run-rate EBIT achieved or credibly bridged by Month 12 with ≥70% of actions already contracted/executed |
| 4 | **Management** | ≥80% of the top 40 retained; a named, credible leadership team willing to sign a 3-year plan |
| 5 | **Cash and truth** | Reported EBITDA reconciled to operating cash within ±15%; no further balance-sheet surprises; working-capital release on plan |

**Then the strategic overlay — decides between "fix and keep" (A) and "fix and sell" (B):**

| Question | Keep | Sell |
|---|---|---|
| Does the core clear the group ROCE hurdle within 24 months? | Yes | No |
| Is the group the **best owner** — does it add density, capability or customers a rival owner could not? | Yes | No |
| Does exit measurably damage crown-jewel group profit (per signed divisional analysis)? | Yes | No |
| Capital and management attention required vs. alternative uses in the group? | Favourable | Unf

### Phase 1 — Fact base and first cuts (Months 2–3)
- Five diagnostic workstreams complete (§2.2). **Day 100: verdict paper to board — structural / execution / mixed, with the defensible core defined at contract level.**
- Exit initiated on unprofitable / low-linkage customers (no veto available) — typically 8–12% of revenue.
- Change-order and claims recovery task force live on the existing project backlog; this is early, high-certainty cash.
- Repricing campaign launched on recurring contracts: escalation restoration, bottom-decile renegotiation.
- Vendor data room opened *internally* as "standalone readiness" — carve-out P&L, TSA scoping, legal entity map, contract assignability review. Presented internally as good management hygiene, which it is.

### Phase 2 — Surgery and proof (Months 4–6)
- Lump-sum installation line: no new bids, orderly completion of existing work, plant disposal program, bonding and parent-guarantee run-off plan agreed with sureties.
- Labour supply: repriced or exited.
- Branch rationalisation decisions taken for the surviving footprint; overhead resized *to surviving revenue* — the opposite of the prior across-the-board programs.
- Shared-customer resolution complete; divisional sign-offs obtained.
- **Confidential market sounding**: 3–5 strategic acquirers and 2–3 sponsors approached via adviser, no-names basis, to establish indicative value ranges and structures.
- Exit-cost floor finalised.

### **Month 6–7 — THE GATE** (see §8)
Board decides: Track A (keep and fix), Track B (fix-and-sell / carve-out), or Track D (orderly exit). All prior work supports all three.

### Phase 3a — If turnaround (Months 7–12)
- Deliver positive run-rate EBIT by Month 10–11; book-to-bill >1.0 in core lines.
- Reinvest: specialty capability, sales hiring, systems for job costing and pricing discipline (the absence of which caused this).
- Re-underwrite as a new business: 3-year plan with capital request judged on its own merits against group hurdle rate — *not* on sunk history.

### Phase 3b — If exit (Months 7–15)
- Months 7–8: adviser mandated, information memorandum, management presentations rehearsed.
- Months 9–11: process run; indicative bids; shortlist; confirmatory diligence.
- Months 12–14: SPA negotiation, TSA, regulatory/works-council consultation, preferred-vendor agreements protecting crown-jewel relationships.
- Month 14–15: close. Retained-liability management thereafter (warranty tails, bonds, environmental).

---

## 7. Exit Alternatives

| Option | Structure | Realistic value | Best when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Whole-unit trade sale** | Sale to a services consolidator | Only credible **after** surgery. Pre-surgery: nominal or negative EV (buyer prices the loss-making lines and liabilities). Post-surgery: 5–7× EBITDA on the core. | Core proven, buyer wants scale/density |
| **2. Carve-out sale of the core** | Sell recurring + specialty ($170M rev, ~$15–18M EBITDA); wind down projects internally | Highest gross proceeds (**~$80–120M**) but group retains the closure cost of the rest | Buyers want the annuity, not the project risk |
| **3. Book-of-business / contract sale** | Sell contracts, customer lists, technicians and local assets by geography to 2–4 regional buyers | $30–60M in aggregate; avoids entity-level liability transfer | No single buyer for the whole; strong regional clusters |
| **4. MBO / sponsor deal** | Retained management, vendor loan, earn-out, group as anchor customer | Modest upfront, meaningful deferred; **highest execution certainty** because the buyer already knows the assets | Management is strong and committed; external buyers are scarce |
| **5. Internal transfer** | Fold the core into the profitable division whose customers it serves; close the rest | No cash proceeds, but eliminates the shared-customer objection entirely and captures real commercial synergy | Group linkage proves genuinely material |
| **6. JV / partial sale** | 50/50 with a larger operator who contributes density and takes management control | Deconsolidation, retained upside, relationship preserved | Sub-scale but strategically relevant |
| **7. Orderly solvent wind-down** | Complete backlog, novate contracts, sell assets, redeploy people, preferred-vendor agreements for crown jewels | **Net cost**, e.g. $60–90M, partly offset by $40–60M working-capital release and disposals | No profitable core exists at any scale |
| **8. Sale-leaseback / asset monetisation** | Applies under *any* track | $20–40M cash | Always evaluate; funds the turnaround without group capital |

**Two rules on exit:**
- **Sequence matters more than option choice.** Every option is worth dramatically more after the loss-making lines are gone. Selling in Month 3 destroys value; the surgery *is* the deal preparation.
- **The wind-down cost is the reservation price.** If orderly closure costs $75M net, a bid of "$0 with full liability assumption" is worth $75M. Boards routinely reject such bids on optics and then spend the $75M anyway.

---

## 8. The Month 6–7 Gate: Explicit Criteria

**All five hard gates must pass for Track A or B (fix). Any two failing → Track D (exit now).**

| # | Gate | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Proven profitable core** | ≥$150M revenue at ≥18% contribution margin, demonstrated on *actual* contract-level data for ≥2 consecutive quarters — not forecast |
| 2 | **Demand** | Core-lines book-to-bill ≥1.0 and improving; ≥85% renewal rate on recurring contracts; no loss of a crown-jewel account |
| 3 | **Run-rate profitability visible** | Positive run-rate EBIT achieved or credibly bridged by Month 12 with ≥70% of actions already contracted/executed |
| 4 | **Management** | ≥80% of the top 40 retained; a named, credible leadership team willing to sign a 3-year plan |
| 5 | **Cash and truth** | Reported EBITDA reconciled to operating cash within ±15%; no further balance-sheet surprises; working-capital release on plan |

**Then the strategic overlay — decides between "fix and keep" (A) and "fix and sell" (B):**

| Question | Keep | Sell |
|---|---|---|
| Does the core clear the group ROCE hurdle within 24 months? | Yes | No |
| Is the group the **best owner** — does it add density, capability or customers a rival owner could not? | Yes | No |
| Does exit measurably damage crown-jewel group profit (per signed divisional analysis)? | Yes | No |
| Capital and management attention required vs. alternative uses in the group? | Favourable | Unf
